title: First difference: avoidability—habitual and assisting grace can shun atrocities, not daily lighter faults
source_text: XXXVIII. In sequentibus autem prolixe recenset varia discrimina inter peccatum quod mortale, & inter illud quod veniale vocat. Et primo quidem dicit peccata mortalia a venialibus differre ratione evitabilitatis, hoc est, ratione virium quas per Dei gratiam habemus ad ea vitanda. Potest enim, inquit, homo regenitus vi & subsidio gratiae, partim internae, seu inhaerentis, quae habitualis dicitur, partim externae seu assistentis, quam gratiam auxilii specialis vocant, potest, inquam, vitare illa carnis opera manifesta, illa peccata atrocia, quae 1 Cor. 6. 9, & 10. & Galat. 5. 19, 20, 21. recensentur. Illa vero leviora peccata, quae venialia vocantur, nullus sanctorum per eam gratiae mensuram quam Deus iis in hac vita admetiri solet, diu vitare potest, nedum toto tempore vitae suae.
pass_a_gloss: In what follows moreover he at length reviews various discriminations between the sin he calls mortal and that which he calls venial. And first indeed he says mortal sins differ from venial by reason of avoidability, that is, by reason of the powers which through God’s grace we have for avoiding them. For, he says, the regenerate man by the force and aid of grace—partly internal or inherent, which is called habitual, partly external or assisting, which they call the grace of special help—can, I say, avoid those manifest works of the flesh, those atrocious sins which are listed in 1 Cor. 6:9–10 and Gal. 5:19–21. But those lighter sins which are called venial no saint, by that measure of grace which God is wont to mete out to them in this life, can long avoid, still less for the whole time of his life.
pass_b_english: Baron’s first cut: avoidability under grace.
Habitual plus assisting grace can keep the regenerate from Paul’s listed atrocities; daily ‘venial’ slips no saint outruns for life.

choices.why: Universal regenerate inability for daily lighter faults.
